articles.title: MP Congress questions Rs 575 Cr aircraft purchase by Mohan Yadav govt amid debt burden; seeks cost details
articles.description: The Congress on Friday questioned the Madhya Pradesh government's purchase of a jet and a helicopter at a reported combined cost of Rs 575 crore amid the state's debt burden and alleged delays in social security pensions and honorarium payments to women's groups preparing Mid-Day Meals. He demanded disclosure of the procurement contracts, payments and additional expenditure. Madhya Pradesh Congress Media Department chairman, Mukesh Nayak, said the reported increase in the prices of the aircraft and expenditure on their interiors raised questions about transparency and the Chief Minister Mohan Yadav-led government's spending priorities."When regular air services are available, why did the government need to purchase such an expensive aircraft and a helicopter using public money?" Nayak asked in a statement. He said the state Cabinet approved the purchases on July 10, 2024. The jet's initial cost of around Rs 234 crore reportedly rose to Rs 350 crore, while the helicopter's price increased from Rs 125 crore to Rs 225 crore. Nayak claimed that around Rs 60 crore was spent on the customisation of the jet's interiors and Rs 20 crore on the helicopter's interiors. He demanded details of expenditure on customs duty, GST, insurance and other components, along with tender documents, contracts and payment records. Questioning the BJP government's priorities amid Madhya Pradesh's debt burden, he cited complaints of delays in social security pensions and honorarium payments to women's groups preparing Mid-Day Meals. He also flagged pending contractor payments and incomplete infrastructure projects."Public money should be spent on people's needs, not on facilities whose necessity and cost themselves raise serious questions," he said. Nayak also referred to the Rs 3,200-crore drinking water scheme in Satna and Maihar, alleging that substantial funds had been withdrawn while villages continued to face water shortages. He demanded details of the work completed and a deadline for the project's completion. He said state Congress president Jitu Patwari had also raised allegations of financial irregularities in the aircraft purchase, including a purported Rs 100-crore commission, and demanded an impartial investigation.

articles.title: Yamuna's Kalindi Kunj stretch covered in foam; AAP questions BJP's cleanup efforts
articles.description: New Delhi: Thick layers of foam covered parts of the Yamuna at Delhi's Kalindi Kunj on Friday, bringing the river's persistent pollution problem into focus ahead of Chhath Puja, when thousands of devotees traditionally gather along its banks to offer prayers. The visuals also triggered political criticism, with AAP leader Saurabh Bharadwaj sharing footage of the foam-covered river and questioning the BJP government's efforts to clean the Yamuna. The development came as the Delhi government outlined its longer-term river rejuvenation programme. On Thursday, Union Home Minister Amit Shah inaugurated and laid the foundation stones for 43 water and sewerage projects worth Rs 8,941 crore, aimed at strengthening sewage treatment and preventing untreated wastewater from entering the river. Shah said the government was working towards cleaning the Yamuna by May 2029. Shah accused the previous Congress and AAP governments of turning the Yamuna into a drain by allowing thousands of tonnes of waste to enter it daily. He asserted that the BJP government was committed to completely cleaning the river before May 2029. Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta, in a post on X on Friday, described the Yamuna as the capital's lifeline and said the government was working to prevent untreated sewage from entering the river while developing cleaner, accessible riverfront spaces. A day earlier, Gupta had termed the launch a significant milestone and said her government had made substantial progress towards river rejuvenation over the past one-and-a-half years. However, AAP Delhi chief Saurabh Bharadwaj challenged the BJP government's claims by sharing visuals of the polluted river on Friday. "By the way, this is today's Yamuna," Bharadwaj wrote on X, addressing Shah. He also questioned the Union Home Minister over the alleged lack of action by investigative agencies in several purported irregularities involving the Delhi government, including DJB tenders, road construction and health-related projects. AAP had earlier raised questions over the tendering process for deploying anti-foaming chemicals at Kalindi Kunj, alleging that arrangements were being made at the site before financial bids were opened. The recurring foam is associated with surfactants from untreated domestic sewage, detergents and industrial discharge. The churning of polluted water near the Okhla barrage, combined with falling temperatures, further intensifies froth formation. Authorities have been preparing to deploy chemical defoaming agents ahead of Chhath Puja, although such measures primarily address visible foam rather than the underlying pollution. While much of the newly announced infrastructure will take time to become operational, Friday's scenes at Kalindi Kunj highlighted the challenge facing the government in translating its ambitious cleanup commitments into measurable improvements in the Yamuna's water quality.

articles.title: Marco Rubio India Visit 2026: US Trade Deal & MSME Impact
articles.description: SMEStreet Exclusive Analysis | As Washington and New Delhi move closer to concluding their long-awaited bilateral trade agreement, Rubio’s engagements in Mumbai and Jamnagar bring trade, energy security, technology, geopolitics and the future of Indian exporters into sharper focus. By Dr Faiz Askari, Founder & Chief Editor, SMEStreet New Delhi, October 21, 2026: When US Secretary of State Marco Rubio arrived in India, the significance of his visit extended far beyond conventional diplomacy. At a time when international trade is increasingly influenced by tariffs, energy disruptions, geopolitical rivalries and changing supply chains, his engagements in Mumbai and Jamnagar have placed India–US economic cooperation at an important crossroads. For India, the visit presents an opportunity to restore momentum to a strategically important relationship that has experienced its share of economic disagreements. For Washington, it is an opportunity to strengthen cooperation with a major economic and geopolitical partner while expanding American commercial interests in energy, defence and technology. For Indian industry, however, the most important question is straightforward: Will the diplomatic optimism translate into commercially meaningful advantages for Indian exporters, manufacturers, service providers and MSMEs? Rubio has indicated that negotiations on the India–US Bilateral Trade Agreement are approaching completion, with only a limited number of issues remaining unresolved. In an interview with The Indian Express, he suggested that approximately 99% of the work had been completed and that finalisation could be a matter of weeks rather than months. Although this offers considerable encouragement, an important distinction remains. A trade agreement approaching completion is not the same as an agreement being signed, ratified and implemented. It is precisely this difference that Indian industry will be watching. Rubio–Jaishankar Meeting: Trade Negotiations Enter a Critical Phase On October 20, Rubio met External Affairs Minister Dr S. Jaishankar in Mumbai, where discussions covered trade, energy security, defence, emerging technologies and wider international developments. Both governments reaffirmed the importance of strengthening the India–US Comprehensive Global Strategic Partnership and welcomed progress in negotiations on the Bilateral Trade Agreement. The discussions also touched upon energy security and developments in the Middle East, demonstrating the extent to which geopolitical challenges have become inseparable from the economic relationship. The visit represents an important effort to rebuild confidence at a time when differences over American tariffs, India's purchases of Russian oil and several trade-related concerns have created uncertainty. The underlying strategic interests, however, remain substantial. India offers the United States a rapidly expanding consumer market, a significant manufacturing base, a large technology workforce and an important role in Indo-Pacific security. The United States, meanwhile, remains a major destination for Indian exports, a source of technology and investment, and a strategically important partner for India's industrial and economic development. The bilateral relationship is therefore too commercially significant to remain hostage to recurring disagreements. How Close Is the India–US Trade Deal? One of the strongest messages emerging from Rubio's visit is that both sides believe a negotiated breakthrough is within reach. The February 2026 trade framework had already provided a basis for reducing some tariff-related tensions. Under that arrangement, Washington announced a reduction in its reciprocal tariff on India to 18%, alongside the removal of an additional 25% tariff associated with Russian oil purchases. Product-specific duties and other trade measures require separate consideration. The negotiations since then have focused on converting the broader understanding into enforceable commitments. On October 15, Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal indicated that the first tranche of the agreement was undergoing final legal drafting. He also made an economically important point: India intends to proceed when the agreement provides its exporters with a competitive or comparable advantage against rival exporting economies. This is particularly relevant because India does not compete in the American market in isolation. Bangladesh, Vietnam, Indonesia and several other economies compete directly with India in products ranging from garments and footwear to consumer goods and manufactured components. If Indian exporters obtain less favourable market-access conditions than their competitors, the commercial value of an agreement could be significantly reduced. Consequently, India is seeking more than tariff reductions. It is seeking a predictable and competitively fair trading environment. What can realistically be expected from the agreement? The immediate priority is likely to be the conclusion of the pending first tranche, including clarity on tariff commitments, preferential market access and the legal language governing implementation. Further progress could emerge in technology trade, energy purchases, customs facilitation, rules of origin, standards recognition and investment cooperation. Nevertheless, expectations should remain measured. The precise benefits for any industry will depend on the final tariff schedules, exemptions, product coverage and implementation provisions. The timing of an announcement is also not guaranteed. Rubio's optimism strengthens the expectation of an early conclusion, but the agreement must still satisfy the commercial and political requirements of both countries. Why This Visit Is Economically More Important Than It Appears According to figures published by the Embassy of India in Washington, bilateral goods and services trade between India and the United States reached approximately $241.66 billion during calendar year 2025. India's merchandise exports to the American market accounted for approximately $103.82 billion, while bilateral services trade exceeded $92 billion. These figures establish the scale of the relationship. A change in tariff treatment, customs procedures or market-access rules can influence billions of dollars in commercial transactions. For Indian businesses, these decisions affect actual order books, pricing negotiations, manufacturing schedules, working capital requirements and employment. For American businesses, India offers opportunities in energy, advanced manufacturing, civil aviation, digital infrastructure, healthcare technologies and defence-related supply chains. However, the trade relationship is not without competing interests. Washington is seeking greater access for American goods and technology, while India must ensure that market-opening commitments do not disproportionately affect vulnerable domestic industries. A successful agreement will therefore have to balance two objectives: strengthening bilateral trade and protecting the competitiveness of strategically important sectors. Jamnagar and the Energy Question: Why Oil Diplomacy Matters Rubio's engagement with Reliance Industries and his visit to the company's Jamnagar refining complex demonstrate how energy security has moved to the centre of contemporary diplomacy. The United States has expressed interest in encouraging increased processing of Venezuelan crude through Indian refining facilities, with potential discussions extending to upstream opportunities. Reliance's substantial refining infrastructure makes Jamnagar strategically relevant to international petroleum trade, particularly during periods of supply disruption. For India, the commercial implications extend beyond a single corporate group. Access to diversified crude supplies can support energy resilience, while stable petroleum availability is important for domestic manufacturing and logistics. Yet diversification is not automatically equivalent to lower energy costs. Shipping expenses, crude quality, refining economics, geopolitical restrictions and global oil prices will continue to determine the actual advantage. For Indian MSMEs, energy diplomacy may appear removed from everyday business operations. Its consequences, however, are immediate. Higher fuel prices increase transportation costs. Expensive petroleum derivatives raise input costs for plastics, chemicals, packaging and several manufacturing sectors. Volatile energy markets complicate pricing and inventory decisions. Greater supply reliability would therefore be beneficial to the wider industrial ecosystem, provided it translates into improved domestic price stability. Rubio's Jamnagar engagement also demonstrates India's increasing importance as an industrial and energy-processing partner rather than merely a large consumer of imported petroleum. The Russian Oil Issue: Can Trade and Strategic Autonomy Coexist? One of the most complicated aspects of India–US relations has been India's continued purchase of Russian crude oil. Washington has sought to use economic pressure in response to the Russia–Ukraine conflict. India, however, has consistently had to consider its own energy requirements, import dependence and economic interests. The recent American waiver of additional sanctions-related tariffs has improved the immediate environment for trade negotiations. Rubio has acknowledged the difficulty of balancing sanctions policy with the economic consequences for partner nations. This development may indicate a more pragmatic approach, but it does not mean that every disagreement over Russian oil has disappeared. For New Delhi, the long-term challenge is to preserve strategic autonomy while maintaining constructive relationships with the United States, Russia, Europe and other major partners. For Washington, the challenge is to deepen cooperation with India without demanding alignment on every foreign-policy issue. A relationship that accommodates such differences could prove more sustainable than one driven by short-term pressure. The outcome matters to Indian industry because geopolitical disagreements can quickly translate into tariffs, sanctions uncertainty, disrupted payment channels and changes in logistics costs. A Changing Global Order: Can India Emerge as a More Important Economic Bridge? Rubio's visit must also be examined against a wider transformation of the international economic system. Globalisation is not disappearing, but its operating principles are changing. Businesses increasingly consider political reliability, energy security, technology access, supply-chain resilience and strategic partnerships alongside traditional factors such as wages and production costs. In this environment, India has an opportunity to position itself as a significant alternative and complementary manufacturing base in global supply chains. India, China and the Indo-Pacific The strategic competition between the United States and China creates opportunities for Indian manufacturing, electronics, speciality chemicals, pharmaceuticals, precision engineering and other sectors. American companies seeking greater geographical diversification may consider increasing procurement from Indian manufacturers. But India cannot expect supply chains to relocate purely because of geopolitics. Manufacturing capacity, infrastructure, productivity, quality certification and cost competitiveness will remain decisive. India's participation in the Quad, alongside the United States, Japan and Australia, also provides a broader strategic framework for cooperation in technology, maritime security and supply-chain resilience. India, the Middle East and global connectivity Rubio and Jaishankar also participated in discussions with the UAE's Foreign Minister, bringing regional energy security and economic connectivity into the diplomatic conversation. This trilateral dimension is significant. India occupies an important position between Asian manufacturing centres, Middle Eastern energy markets, European consumers and American technology ecosystems. Better connectivity and deeper investment partnerships could increase India's role in emerging trade corridors. For Indian businesses, the opportunity lies in converting these diplomatic relationships into commercially viable logistics networks, investment flows and export orders. India's strategic autonomy will remain essential New Delhi's economic ambitions require partnerships across multiple regions. A closer relationship with Washington need not eliminate India's engagement with other markets or multilateral groupings. Instead, India's advantage could lie in its ability to maintain diversified international partnerships while building domestic industrial strength. That is a more sustainable route towards becoming an influential global manufacturing and trading economy. What Will Indian Industry Gain from Rubio's Visit? The commercial benefits will differ substantially across sectors. Textiles, garments and leather: Export-oriented manufacturers could benefit from improved tariff competitiveness and predictable market access. These labour-intensive industries are especially sensitive to small changes in landed costs. Engineering and auto components: Indian suppliers could gain from stronger procurement relationships, manufacturing partnerships and reduced trade uncertainty. However, sector-specific American tariffs, including those applying to some metal products, will remain important. Pharmaceuticals and healthcare: Opportunities may expand through regulatory cooperation, pharmaceutical supply-chain integration and investment. At the same time, domestic manufacturers will need to monitor changes in intellectual-property, regulatory and market-access provisions. IT and digital services: Closer technology cooperation could support artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, cloud infrastructure and digital transformation. Nevertheless, trade progress will not automatically resolve difficulties arising from American immigration and visa policies. Electronics and semiconductors: India's ambition to expand advanced manufacturing may receive additional momentum through technology investment, component sourcing and deeper industrial partnerships. Defence and aerospace: Cooperation could generate opportunities for Indian component manufacturers and specialist engineering firms, depending on procurement arrangements, technology-transfer conditions and localisation requirements. Energy and petrochemicals: Increased commercial cooperation may support refining, storage, logistics, equipment manufacturing and downstream industrial activity. Agriculture and food processing: Certain export opportunities may improve, but sensitive domestic agricultural and dairy interests will require careful protection. Market-opening commitments must account for the livelihoods of Indian producers and processors. The broad conclusion is that the proposed agreement could create significant openings, but its gains will not be evenly distributed. What Are Indian Industry Leaders Saying? Industry perspectives reveal a combination of optimism about American demand and concern about the practical cost of doing business. Recent comments reported by The Financial Express on October 21 highlight the resilience of Indian engineering exporters, as well as the uneven impact of tariffs across large and smaller businesses. Pankaj Chadha, Chairman of EEPC India, has pointed to continuing demand from the American market. His assessment reflects the importance of long-established commercial relationships between Indian suppliers and American buyers. Arun Kumar Garodia, Managing Director of Corona Steel and former EEPC India President, has explained that exporters already integrated into American supply chains can be difficult to replace because buyers must consider quality, logistics and established supplier relationships. These observations indicate that Indian manufacturing possesses strengths extending beyond low-cost production. However, the MSME perspective is more challenging. Khalid Khan, a Mumbai-based engine-parts exporter, has highlighted the severe impact of freight costs on smaller exporters, indicating that broad sectoral growth figures may conceal financial stress among smaller businesses. S. C. Ralhan, President of the Federation of Indian Export Organisations (FIEO), has described how exporters and American buyers shared tariff-related costs to maintain their business relationships. He has also raised concerns about the slow pace of tariff-refund processes. These are reported industry assessments of current export conditions, not statements made specifically in response to Rubio's visit. Taken together, they illustrate what industry will be looking for from the proposed agreement: tariff predictability, commercially competitive access, lower transaction costs and faster resolution of trade-related difficulties. For trade bodies such as FIEO, CII, FICCI, ASSOCHAM and the export promotion councils, a commercially meaningful agreement would create an opportunity to promote investment, expand exports and encourage international business partnerships. However, the benefits must reach beyond large corporations. The MSME Perspective: Will Small Businesses Actually Benefit? India's MSMEs are deeply connected to the country's export economy. Many operate as direct exporters, while others supply materials, components, specialised services and manufacturing capabilities to larger exporting companies. An improvement in India–US trade relations can therefore influence thousands of businesses that may never negotiate directly with an American importer. The opportunities can be substantial. 1. Greater access to American buyers A predictable tariff environment could allow smaller Indian exporters to approach American buyers with greater confidence. Industries such as home furnishings, engineering goods, processed foods, handicrafts, garments and auto components could benefit from more competitive pricing. But smaller businesses will need assistance in identifying buyers and meeting procurement requirements. 2. Opportunities within global value chains Not every MSME needs to become a direct exporter. An Indian precision-engineering unit, packaging supplier or electronic-component manufacturer can benefit by joining the supply chain of a larger exporter or multinational manufacturer. This supplier-led model could be particularly relevant for MSMEs in industrial clusters. 3. Increased confidence in manufacturing investment Uncertain tariffs discourage businesses from investing in machinery, capacity expansion and export-specific product development. Greater policy stability may encourage MSMEs to undertake longer-term investments. Such decisions, however, will still depend on access to affordable finance and sufficient order visibility. 4. Technology and productivity improvements Closer cooperation in industrial technology could make advanced machinery, automation systems and digital manufacturing solutions more accessible. For small manufacturers, the challenge will be affordability and practical adoption. Technology partnerships should ideally include skill development, training and MSME-focused capacity-building programmes. 5. Continuing challenges in compliance and finance Even a favourable trade agreement will not automatically solve the structural difficulties faced by smaller exporters. Product certification, testing requirements, international logistics, insurance, working capital, currency fluctuations and delayed payments can substantially affect profitability. Rules of origin and documentation requirements can also become barriers if smaller manufacturers lack the resources to comply. The real measure of success will therefore be whether the agreement makes international trade genuinely easier for smaller enterprises. What India Should Negotiate for Its MSMEs India has an opportunity to place the interests of smaller manufacturers and exporters more visibly within its trade strategy. First, tariff predictability should be a priority. MSMEs need to know the duties that will apply when goods reach American ports, rather than being exposed to sudden changes after production commitments are made. Second, export credit mechanisms should be strengthened. Competitive trade agreements create opportunities, but businesses cannot fulfil new orders without working capital. Third, standards and certification cooperation deserve greater attention. Easier access to internationally accepted testing and conformity-assessment systems could reduce compliance expenses. Fourth, sector-specific buyer–seller programmes should support MSMEs. American procurement organisations and Indian industrial clusters could be brought together through targeted business-matching initiatives. Fifth, technology cooperation should include smaller companies. Skill development, digital manufacturing, cybersecurity and productivity-enhancement initiatives should become practical components of commercial engagement. Finally, India should establish a mechanism to review MSME outcomes after implementation. The success of the agreement should be measured through new exporters, additional orders, higher value addition and sustainable employment—not solely through headline trade values. These measures could help convert a high-level diplomatic agreement into a practical instrument for enterprise development. Three Possible Outcomes for the Trade Deal The future of the negotiations can broadly be assessed through three scenarios. Scenario One: An Early Agreement with Meaningful Market Access If both countries conclude the agreement in the coming weeks and secure competitive terms for key industries, Indian exporters could experience improved business sentiment, stronger buyer enquiries and renewed investment interest. MSMEs integrated into established export supply chains may benefit first. Scenario Two: A Limited Agreement with Further Negotiations A narrower first-stage agreement may reduce uncertainty without resolving every sectoral concern. Under this scenario, businesses could see gradual improvements, while more complicated matters such as agriculture, digital trade and sector-specific tariffs remain subjects of subsequent negotiations. Scenario Three: Continued Delays or Renewed Trade Friction If disagreements over market access, tariffs or geopolitical issues resurface, exporters may continue to face uncertainty. For smaller businesses, the consequences could include delayed investments, pressure on margins and an increased need to diversify export markets. At present, public statements from both governments favour an early negotiated outcome. However, the final text will determine the actual commercial benefits. What Should Indian MSMEs Do Now? Indian exporters should treat the current diplomatic progress as an opportunity to prepare rather than assume that every proposed concession is already available. Businesses dependent on the American market should review their product-level tariff exposure, reassess pricing agreements and examine whether existing contracts adequately address changes in customs duties. Manufacturers planning expansion should strengthen quality systems, compliance documentation and supplier traceability. Industry associations and export promotion councils can play an important role in helping MSMEs interpret the final agreement once it is announced. Businesses should also continue exploring alternative international markets. The objective should not be to replace dependence on one market with dependence on another. It should be to build a diversified and resilient export strategy. For MSMEs, trade diplomacy creates the opportunity. Business preparedness determines how much of that opportunity can actually be captured. SMEStreet's Analysis: A Strategic Opportunity That Must Deliver at the Enterprise Level Marco Rubio's visit comes at a consequential time for India–US relations. The relationship is moving through a period in which economic cooperation, technology partnerships and geopolitical calculations increasingly influence one another. India has advantages that make it important to Washington: its market size, manufacturing potential, technology capabilities, geopolitical position and expanding international influence. The United States remains equally important to India's ambitions in trade, investment, advanced technology and industrial development. The opportunity for both countries lies in recognising that these interests are often complementary, even when their positions on individual policy matters differ. From India's standpoint, however, success should not be defined merely by a signing ceremony or the announcement of another high-profile bilateral understanding. An effective agreement must create measurable improvements in market access, investment confidence, technology cooperation and industrial competitiveness. Above all, it should provide smaller businesses with opportunities that have traditionally been easier for larger enterprises to capture. The next important development will be the finalisation of the trade agreement and the publication of its commercially relevant terms. If Rubio's visit helps move India and the United States from diplomatic assurances towards predictable and mutually beneficial trade commitments, it may be remembered as an important turning point. But its lasting economic significance will ultimately be judged not only in Washington and New Delhi, but also in the factories, workshops, industrial clusters and export offices where Indian entrepreneurs make their daily commercial decisions. For India's MSME economy, that is where the real India–US trade story begins. About the Author Dr Faiz Askari is the Founder and Chief Editor of SMEStreet.in, a business media platform focused on India's MSME ecosystem, entrepreneurship, industry development, policy and international trade. Through SMEStreet, he works to connect business leaders, policymakers, industry associations and emerging enterprises while highlighting opportunities for sustainable economic growth. articles.title: MP: Viral video of ACS over civic body purchases sparks controversy
articles.description: A video showing Madhya Pradesh Additional Chief Secretary Sanjay Dubey pulling up officials over alleged irregularities in purchases by urban local bodies has surfaced on social media, with the senior bureaucrat warning of strict action against discrepancies in procurement. The viral video is reportedly from a review meeting held at a training institute in Bhowri, Bhopal, where Dubey discussed purchases made through the Government e-Marketplace (GeM) portal by urban local bodies over the past three years. According to an analysis presented at the meeting, 374 urban local bodies made purchases worth Rs 1,134 crore through the portal during the period. The analysis pointed to substantial price differences in the procurement of similar goods and equipment. Citing an example, Dubey said one urban local body had purchased a garbage collection vehicle for Rs 2 lakh, while another had paid Rs 6 lakh for a similar vehicle fitted with an additional dustbin. The analysis estimated that the state government could have saved around Rs 250 crore if the purchases had been made at average rates. The figure represents estimated potential savings and does not, by itself, establish the extent of any proven financial loss or corruption. Dubey warned officials that strict punitive action would be taken if irregularities were found in procurement from this year onwards. The episode has brought scrutiny to purchasing practices in urban local bodies and the monitoring of public expenditure. Reacting to the issue, Madhya Pradesh Congress president Jitu Patwari criticised the state government over its debt and the proposed expenditure on an aircraft for the Chief Minister."History will be ashamed that when Madhya Pradesh was burdened with a debt of Rs 6 lakh crore, the Chief Minister was spending Rs 350 crore on a single aircraft to fulfil his personal preferences," Patwari said. He accused the BJP of allowing corruption to spread in the state, describing it as a "cancer of corruption", and called for the party to be removed from power at all levels, from village sarpanches to Members of Parliament. Responding to a IANS query on Thursday, Minister of State for Urban Development and Housing Pratima Bagri said proper supervision and regular monitoring were necessary to identify irregularities. She said the state government had taken action in similar cases in the past and would continue to take appropriate action against wrongdoing.--IANSpd/dan

articles.title: TN govt fixes Rs 26 lakh car purchase ceiling for ministers, Rs 15 lakh for MLAs
articles.description: The Tamil Nadu government has fixed a ceiling of Rs 26 lakh for purchasing official cars for ministers and senior legislative functionaries, while setting a Rs 15 lakh limit for other MLAs under revised rules governing vehicle entitlements. The changes have been notified through a new gazette amending the travelling allowance rules applicable to members of the Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly. The notification lays down purchase limits, procurement procedures, ownership arrangements and conditions for returning government vehicles. Apart from ministers, the Rs 26 lakh ceiling will apply to the Speaker, Deputy Speaker, Leader of the Opposition and Government Chief Whip. All other Assembly members will be eligible for vehicles costing up to Rs 15 lakh. The prescribed limits cover the total purchase cost, including the vehicleâ€™s ex-showroom price, taxes, registration charges and motor insurance premiums. These expenses must therefore be accommodated within the applicable ceiling, rather than treated as additional payments. The government order also provides for a five per cent annual increase in the purchase ceilings, allowing the permissible expenditure to rise each year. Vehicles allotted to ministers will be purchased by the Tamil Nadu government in its own name. Procurement for the Speaker, Deputy Speaker, Leader of the Opposition, Government Chief Whip and other legislators will be handled through the Assembly Secretariat. All vehicles purchased under the amended rules must comply with Bharat Stage VI emission standards. Purchases must be made through the Union governmentâ€™s Government e-Marketplace, or GeM, portal, according to the notification. Ministers must return their allotted vehicles to the government when they leave office, complete their tenure or lose their positions for reasons including disqualification. Similar provisions governing the return of vehicles have been prescribed for the Speaker and other eligible office-holders. For ordinary MLAs, expenditure on vehicle upkeep, repairs, fuel and driving will have to be met from the vehicle allowance payable to them under the applicable rules. The amended provisions thus distinguish the purchase of vehicles from the recurring expenses associated with their use. The government order introducing the amendments was issued by Public Department Secretary E. Sundaravalli. The revised framework specifies both the financial entitlement of each category of legislator and the administrative responsibility for procuring vehicles, while making continued possession subject to the conditions attached to holding the relevant office.--IANSaal/dan
